mentor.diagnosis: You mixed up the per incident figure with the yearly figure, or forgot the exposure factor.
contrast: Asset value, what the whole thing is worth
Exposure factor, the fraction lost in one event
Single loss expectancy, cost of one event
Annualized rate of occurrence, events per year
Given, 0.5 means once every two years
Annualized loss expectancy, cost per year
mentor.rule: SLE is one event, ALE is one year. A control is worth buying when it costs less than the ALE it removes.
mentor.tell: 'Once every four years' is an ARO of 0.25, not 4. That single conversion is the most common arithmetic slip.
mentor.trap: If the exposure factor is omitted from your working, SLE equals the asset value and every downstream number is wrong but still looks plausible.

label: RTO vs RPO vs MTTR vs MTBF

mentor.diagnosis: You read one of these as another. Two are targets you choose, two are measurements you observe.
contrast: How long until service is back, a target
How much data you can afford to lose, a target
How long repairs actually take, observed
mentor.rule: RPO points backwards and sets your backup frequency. RTO points forwards and sets your recovery capability. RPO of one hour means backups at least hourly.
mentor.tell: 'We can lose at most 15 minutes of transactions' is an RPO. 'We must be trading again within 4 hours' is an RTO.
mentor.trap: Both are stated in units of time in the same sentence of a BIA, so the numbers are easy to swap.

label: Risk appetite vs risk tolerance vs risk threshold

mentor.diagnosis: You used appetite and tolerance as synonyms. Appetite is strategic and broad, tolerance is the acceptable variance around it.
contrast: How much risk the organisation wants to take pursuing its goals
The board, as expansionary, conservative or neutral
How much variance from that is acceptable in practice
The specific line that triggers action
mentor.rule: Appetite is the strategy, tolerance is the wobble allowed, threshold is the trip wire.
mentor.tell: Expansionary, conservative and neutral are appetite words.
mentor.trap: In everyday speech the two words mean the same thing, so the distinction feels invented. The exam still tests it.

label: Transfer vs accept vs avoid vs mitigate

mentor.diagnosis: You named a treatment that does not match what the organisation actually did with the risk.
contrast: Deploy MFA to reduce credential theft
Financial impact moved to a third party
Buy cyber insurance, or outsource the function
The activity is stopped, so the risk no longer exists
Cancel the product line that required storing card data
Acknowledged and nothing further is done
Documented as an exception, signed off by the risk owner
mentor.rule: Avoid removes the activity. Mitigate reduces the risk. Transfer moves who pays. Accept does nothing but write it down.
mentor.tell: Insurance is always transfer. Discontinuing the service is always avoid. Note that transfer moves the financial impact, not the accountability.
mentor.trap: Outsourcing feels like avoidance because the work leaves the building. The risk still exists and you remain accountable for it, so it is transfer.

mentor.diagnosis: You classified the analysis by how rigorous it felt rather than by whether it produces currency figures.
contrast: High, medium, low; a heat map
Asset values and reliable frequency data
Reputational and safety risks that resist pricing
Comparing a control's cost against the loss it prevents
False precision when the input data is guessed
mentor.rule: If the answer is a number in currency, it is quantitative. If it is a word or a colour on a matrix, it is qualitative.
mentor.tell: SLE, ARO, ALE and exposure factor are all quantitative. A 5 by 5 likelihood and impact grid is qualitative.
mentor.trap: Qualitative sounds like the weaker method, so it looks wrong. It is the right method when the impact genuinely cannot be priced.

label: Business impact analysis vs risk assessment

mentor.diagnosis: You confused the exercise that identifies threats with the one that measures what disruption costs.
contrast: What could go wrong and how likely is it
If this process stops, how bad is it and how fast must it return
A risk register with likelihood and impact
Business continuity and disaster recovery plans
mentor.rule: Risk assessment asks what might happen. BIA assumes it already happened and asks what it costs per hour.
mentor.tell: Anything producing RTO or RPO figures is a BIA. Anything producing likelihood ratings is a risk assessment.
mentor.trap: Both analyse impact, and both feed planning. The BIA is deliberately indifferent to cause, which is the cleanest way to separate them.

label: Ad hoc vs recurring vs one-time vs continuous assessment

mentor.diagnosis: You matched on how thorough each sounds. They differ by what triggers them, and the trigger is what the stem always gives you.
contrast: An event: an acquisition, a breach, a new regulation
Something changed that the schedule did not anticipate
Keeping the risk register current as a matter of routine
A specific decision or project, with a defined end
Assessing a single new supplier or a migration
Always on, automated, fed by tooling
Cloud posture, vulnerability state, control monitoring
mentor.rule: Ad hoc is unscheduled and event-driven. One-time is scheduled once for a defined purpose. The difference is whether anyone planned it.
mentor.tell: An acquisition or an incident points to ad hoc. An annual cycle points to recurring. A tool watching posture constantly points to continuous.
mentor.trap: Ad hoc and one-time are the pair people swap. A one-time assessment is deliberately scoped and planned for a purpose; an ad hoc assessment is a response to something that just happened.

label: Expansionary, conservative and neutral risk appetite

mentor.diagnosis: You judged these as degrees of competence rather than as deliberate positions. A high appetite is a strategy, not a failure of governance.
contrast: Willing to accept more risk in pursuit of growth or opportunity
A startup entering a market, aggressive product launch
Prefers to minimise risk even at the cost of opportunity
Balanced: accepts risk where the return justifies it
Most established organisations, most of the time
mentor.rule: Appetite is how much risk the organisation is willing to take to achieve its objectives, set by the board. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around that in practice, and the threshold is the line that triggers action.
mentor.tell: A stem describing strategy and growth rather than a specific control decision.
mentor.trap: Expansionary is not recklessness. The exam expects you to read it as a deliberate, governed choice, which is why it appears as a named posture rather than as a criticism.

label: A risk exception vs a risk exemption

mentor.diagnosis: You used the two words interchangeably. Both permit a departure from policy, and they differ in whether the departure is meant to end.
contrast: Temporary, with an expiry and a review date
Ongoing, for a case the policy was never meant to cover
The gap is permanent and accepted
Owner, justification, and formal sign-off at the right level
Renewed indefinitely until it is an exemption nobody approved
Granted casually, so policy quietly stops meaning anything
mentor.rule: An exception has an end date. An exemption does not. If the stem mentions a review date or a plan to remediate, it is an exception.
mentor.tell: Unsupported software kept for a named replacement date points to an exception. A system that will never meet the standard by its nature points to an exemption.
mentor.trap: An exception renewed four times is an undocumented exemption. The exam's interest is that both require an owner and a record, so neither is the same as simply ignoring the finding.

label: Likelihood vs probability vs impact vs exposure factor

mentor.diagnosis: You treated likelihood and probability as one word and impact as a single number. In this objective they belong to different halves of the analysis.
contrast: A qualitative judgement: rare, possible, likely
A number or percentage, or a rate per year
Either a rating or a monetary figure, depending on the method
The proportion of an asset's value lost in one occurrence
mentor.rule: Risk is likelihood combined with impact. Qualitative work uses words and a matrix; quantitative work uses numbers and produces SLE, ARO and ALE. Exposure factor only exists on the quantitative side.
mentor.tell: A scale of high, medium and low points to qualitative. A percentage of asset value or a figure per year points to quantitative.
mentor.trap: Qualitative analysis is often treated as the inferior version. It is the right method when reliable numbers do not exist, and inventing numbers to look rigorous is the worse error.
